__  AI, Data & Analytics__

__SKILLS COVERED IN THIS CLUSTER__

Artificial Intelligence  ·  Agentic AI  ·  Analytics  ·  Data Engineering  ·  Emerging Technologies  ·  Research  ·  Secondary Research  ·  Case Study

★  Priority skills: Artificial Intelligence \(MC\), Analytics \(MC\), Data Engineering \(MC\), Agentic AI \(Developing — rapidly rising\)

📌  *This cluster has the lowest total priority score \(38\.6\) partly due to most skills being at baseline MV \(5\.0\) — reflecting that market data on these skills is still maturing\. However, Artificial Intelligence and Agentic AI are the fastest\-moving skills in the entire Nagarro portfolio\. Course content here will need the most frequent updating\.*

__📚  RECOMMENDED TEXTBOOKS__

- __Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach — Russell & Norvig \(4th ed\., 2020\) — __The definitive university AI textbook, used in virtually every top\-tier AI course globally\. Covers problem\-solving, knowledge representation, ML, NLP, and robotics\. Technical but accessible to analytically minded business professionals\.
- __Deep Learning — Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville \(2016, free online\) — __Endorsed by Elon Musk as 'the only comprehensive book\.' The technical bible for neural networks\. For practitioners and data engineers who need to understand what's under the hood\. Available free at deeplearningbook\.org\.
- __Competing in the Age of AI — Iansiti & Lakhani, HBS \(2020\) — __The best business\-school text on AI strategy\. Covers how AI\-first operating architectures remove traditional scale constraints\. Winner of Financial Times Business Book of the Year nomination\. Ideal for the Analytics skill in a business context\.
- __Hands\-On Machine Learning with Scikit\-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow — Aurélien Géron \(3rd ed\., 2022\) — __The most practical ML textbook for professionals who want to build, not just understand\. Clear, well\-structured, and Python\-based\. Widely used in applied ML courses\.
- __The Book of Why — Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie \(2018\) — __The foundational text on causal inference in AI/ML — critical for data engineering and analytics\. Pearl's contribution underlies modern AI reasoning\. Accessible to non\-mathematicians\.
- __All\-In on AI — Tom Davenport & Nitin Mittal, Deloitte \(2023\) — __The practitioner's companion to Iansiti & Lakhani\. Profiles companies going all\-in on AI transformation\. Excellent for Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies skills\.

__🎓  UNIVERSITY COURSES__

- __Stanford HAI — Human\-Centered AI Institute \(Fei\-Fei Li, Christopher Manning\) — __Stanford's flagship AI institute\. Free online content on responsible AI\. Stanford CS229 \(Machine Learning, Andrew Ng\) is the most popular course in Stanford history with 1,000\+ students/year\. Lecture videos on YouTube\.
- __MIT — Professional Education: Applied Data Science Program — __4\-course online program covering ML, deep learning, data engineering, and business application\. Grounded in MIT research\. Strong practitioner track record\.
- __Wharton Online — AI for Business \(Wharton Executive Education\) — __Non\-technical AI strategy course for business leaders\. Covers AI deployment, analytics in decision\-making, and transformation\. Ideal for Analytics and Agentic AI skills\.
- __DeepLearning\.AI \(Andrew Ng\) — Coursera Specializations — __Over 150 programs from one\-hour short courses to professional certificates\. AI for Everyone is the best entry point for non\-technical professionals\. Machine Learning Specialization is the world's most popular ML course \(8M\+ students\)\.
- __fast\.ai — Practical Deep Learning for Coders — __Jeremy Howard's free course\. Bottom\-up, code\-first approach\. Best for data engineers who need practical implementation skills\. Free and used by professionals at major tech firms\.

__👩‍🏫  LEADING PROFESSORS__

- __Andrew Ng — __Stanford \(adjunct\), Founder DeepLearning\.AI, Co\-founder Coursera\. Named to TIME 100 Most Influential 2012 and TIME100 AI 2023\. The single most impactful AI educator globally\. His CS229 course and DeepLearning\.AI specializations have taught 8M\+ students\.
- __Fei\-Fei Li — __Stanford HAI, Co\-Director\. Creator of ImageNet\. 'Godmother of AI\.' Pioneer in computer vision and human\-centered AI\. Former VP/Chief Scientist at Google Cloud AI\. Strong advocate for ethical AI\.
- __Yoshua Bengio — __Université de Montréal / MILA\. Turing Award winner \(with Hinton & LeCun, 2018\)\. The most cited academic in deep learning\. Founder of Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms\. Focuses on foundational deep learning and AI safety\.
- __Yann LeCun — __NYU \(Silver Professor\) \+ Chief AI Scientist at Meta\. Turing Award winner\. Invented convolutional neural networks \(CNNs\)\. The architect of modern computer vision\. Actively publishes and lectures\.
- __Andrej Karpathy — __Formerly Tesla, OpenAI\. Founded Eureka Labs \(2024\) to democratize LLM education\. His YouTube lectures on neural networks and LLMs \(e\.g\., 3\.5\-hour ChatGPT explainer, Feb 2025\) are among the clearest technical teaching available anywhere\.
- __Marco Iansiti — __Harvard Business School\. Author of Competing in the Age of AI\. Research: AI business strategy, platform economics, AI governance\. The best academic bridge between AI technology and business leadership\.

__🎬  VIDEOS & ONLINE COURSES__

__🎬  VIDEOS & ONLINE COURSES__

- __Andrew Ng — AI for Everyone \(Coursera, free to audit\) — __The best non\-technical AI orientation for business professionals\. Covers AI capabilities, project management, strategy, and organizational transformation\. ~6 hours total\.
- __Andrej Karpathy — 'Let's Build GPT from Scratch' \(YouTube, 2023\) — __The most cited technical explainer of large language models\. 3\.5 hours\. Demystifies LLMs at the level of matrix math and gradient descent\. Transformative for data engineers\.
- __fast\.ai — Practical Deep Learning for Coders \(free, YouTube \+ website\) — __Jeremy Howard's free course\. Best code\-first, top\-down approach to ML\. Used by Kaggle winners and industry professionals\.
- __Two Minute Papers \(YouTube, 1\.72M subscribers\) — __Károly Zsolnai\-Fehér\. Converts cutting\-edge AI research papers into 2\-minute digestible overviews\. The best channel for staying current on AI breakthroughs\.
- __DeepLearning\.AI YouTube Channel \(Andrew Ng\) — __Structured tutorials, expert interviews, short courses on GenAI, LLMs, MLOps, and AI strategy\. University\-standard quality with practitioner relevance\.
- __Lex Fridman Podcast \(YouTube\) — __Long\-form interviews with AI researchers including Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, Demis Hassabis, Sam Altman\. Deep, unfiltered, and current\.

__📰  KEY ARTICLES & REPORTS__

- __HBR — 'Competing in the Age of AI' — Iansiti & Lakhani \(2019\) — __The original article that became the book\. Argues AI fundamentally changes competitive dynamics\. Essential framing for the Analytics skill in a business strategy context\.
- __McKinsey Global Institute — 'The Age of AI' \(annual\) — __Annual tracker of AI adoption, productivity impact, and workforce implications\. The most reliable industry data on AI's business impact\. Free to download\.
- __Andrew Ng — 'AI Is the New Electricity' \(Stanford GSB, 2017\) — __Ng's most\-cited essay on AI's transformative role\. Sets the strategic context for any AI course\.
- __HBR — 'What AI Can and Can't Do Yet' — Brynjolfsson & Mitchell \(2017, evergreen\) — __Precise framework for where AI excels vs\. where it fails\. Structured decomposition of tasks\. Essential for anyone managing AI projects or vendors\.
- __The Batch — Andrew Ng's weekly newsletter \(deeplearning\.ai/the\-batch\) — __The best weekly digest of AI developments, curated by Ng\. Practical and balanced\. Recommend to all learners as ongoing reading\.

source: E:\Internship-Folder\Prof. Gene\webapp\Vault\raw\Being Human in age of AI.md
content:
Abstract
The growing diffusion of automation in the marketplace affects consumers in two ways. First, marketing activities such as pricing and customer support are increasingly being automated; this automation of marketing activities has profound effects on consumer welfare and well-being. Second, various aspects or types of consumption activities are also being automated; users may automate elements of writing tasks using large language models (LLMs), they may outsource product search to recommender systems, or they may adopt autonomous features in products (e.g., self-driving cars). This JACR issue on Automation of Marketing and Consumption brings together an exciting set of researchers to explore these topics. In this introduction, we reflect on the role of automation in creating value for both consumers and firms, highlight the themes running through the articles in this issue, and offer reflections on possible directions for future research on consumer behavior and psychology in the face of automation and, in particular, artificial intelligence (AI).

What began with clunky telephone menus and evolved into clumsy chatbots and more or less sophisticated scoring and recommendation algorithms is now moving toward fully automated personalization of most aspects of interacting with customers and managing their experiences. In everyday language, much of this automation is now being referred to as artificial intelligence (AI), although arguably not all of it is AI. Over the last decade, a rapidly growing literature in marketing and consumer behavior has examined consumer behavior in response to algorithms that provide predictions, classifications, or recommendations for, or make decisions about, consumers. Such algorithms, or decision rules, have evolved from conventional statistical models specified by humans (e.g., regression or logit models fitted to well-defined sets of variables) to adaptive machine-learning models that not only describe the relationships between variables but also identify the relevant variables to perform those tasks (e.g., in analyzing and classifying images composed of pixels as data points). Machine learning is a subfield of “artificial intelligence,” a more general term that encompasses computer models and hardware that mimic aspects of human intelligence including autonomous learning, reasoning, problem solving, and creativity, as well as sensory and perceptual processes that provide the input into these intelligent activities. AI is made up of algorithms, but not all algorithms are AI.

We begin by offering an overview of the articles in this issue. Together, they take a flexible view of how automation is conceptualized, from simple algorithms to AI. We broadly subsume the articles into two subsets, one that explores effects that automation and AI can have on various aspects of consumer welfare, the other on how different characteristics of automation and AI moderate consumer preferences for using them.

Marketing and Consumer Welfare
One important motivation for consumer researchers investigating the automation of marketing and consumption activities lies in the desire to explore and detail potential risks for consumer welfare. Firms laud the benefits of personalization that marketing automation can deliver to consumers. They can better tailor various aspects of the marketing mix such as advertising, recommendations, or product curations to individual customers’ preferences (e.g., Arora et al. 2008; Lambrecht and Tucker 2013). Recent research suggests that such personalization may enhance consumer welfare in the absence of price discrimination (Korganbekova and Zuber 2023). Yet research has also explored the welfare effects of personalized pricing, that is, price-discriminating between individual customers. Using data from a randomized controlled field experiment with a business-to-business online recruiting service, Dubé and Misra (2023) showed that such personalized pricing not only increased expected seller profits as should be expected, but it also allowed 60% of customers to benefit from lower prices, compared to standardized pricing. Notably, though, overall consumer surplus declined—perhaps not surprisingly when individualized pricing approaches the theoretical ideal of first-degree price discrimination (Wertenbroch 2019). Taking a privacy angle on consumer welfare, Tomaino, Wertenbroch, and Walters’s (2023) experimental findings suggest that consumers value their private data, which platforms need to implement personalization, less when they barter these data for goods and services—as they do on online platforms—than if they were paid in their cash equivalent of these goods and services. This violation of procedure invariance in measuring valuations reveals a cognitive bias in privacy preferences induced by the medium of exchange (barter vs. cash) and suggests an associated reduction of consumer welfare.

These findings paint a nuanced picture of how various aspects of marketing automation affect consumer welfare from an economic and decision-theoretic perspective. Four articles in this issue of JACR complement this economic perspective with similarly nuanced psychological views of consumer welfare, with the goal either of preventing deleterious consequences for consumer welfare emerging from the deployment of algorithms in tasks previously performed by humans or of highlighting ways in which marketers can leverage automation to increase consumer welfare.

source: E:\Internship-Folder\Prof. Gene\webapp\Vault\raw\Being Human in age of AI.md
content:
An example is provided by Valenzuela and colleagues (2024), who explore how AI constrains the range of experiences available to consumers. In the realm of digital consumption, where decisions and experiences are increasingly shaped by algorithms, the integration of LLMs and AI is seen as a double-edged sword. While AI promises to enhance consumer life by making decisions more efficient and experiences more tailored and enjoyable—thanks to recommender systems like Netflix or productivity tools like ChatGPT—it also poses risks that extend beyond the often-discussed concerns of discrimination and privacy. This article dives into the less explored psychological tensions consumers face with AI, focusing on how AI might limit individuals’ expressive range, choices, and personal development opportunities. The concept of “possibility space” is central to the discussion, positing that the pervasive use of AI could narrow human experience by imposing experiential constraints through three mechanisms: agency transference (AI’s tendency to restrict one’s exercise of personal agency), parametric reductionism (AI’s reduction of human complexity into quantifiable metrics), and regulated expression (the limits to human expression that emerge in human-AI interactions, and emerging from design choices or technological limitations). The authors call for a multidisciplinary effort to ensure that AI technologies empower consumers, emphasizing the need for a critical examination of how AI interactions during the customer journey may inadvertently reduce or restrict consumer experiences, thereby challenging human agency and motivation.

While Valenzuela et al.’s (2024) conceptual analysis takes a broad swipe at the topic of automation and consumer welfare, two other empirical articles in this issue take a narrower perspective. Duani, Barasch, and Morwitz (2024) investigate consumer perceptions of fairness in price discrimination based on demographic factors, focusing on whether the discrimination is executed by humans or algorithms. The research reveals that consumers find demographic-based price discrimination to be fairer when it is conducted by algorithms rather than humans. This perception is attributed to consumers feeling less judged by algorithms and believing that algorithmic decisions are less exploitative and more justified. Interestingly, this favorable view toward algorithmic pricing diminishes in scenarios involving more common and less contentious forms of price discrimination, such as time-based pricing, and when the price discrimination aims to achieve a prosocial goal. The study emphasizes the nuanced consumer responses to price discrimination practices in the digital age, highlighting the potential for algorithms to reshape notions of fairness in the marketplace. This work sheds light on critical considerations for consumer welfare, suggesting that while algorithmic price discrimination might mitigate feelings of unfair judgment compared to human-based methods, the implications for consumer welfare are complex and context-dependent.

Consumer welfare is a function of choices by firms, policy makers, and individual consumers. Drawing attention to the importance of the latter, Agarwal and colleagues (2024) take a nuanced approach to understanding consumer preferences for automation by examining the role of self-serving biases as a novel barrier to consumer adoption of autonomous vehicles. They demonstrate that consumers prefer lower levels of vehicle automation for themselves compared to what they prefer for others. This discrepancy is mediated by self-enhancing comparative evaluations, where consumers perceive themselves as safer and more trustworthy drivers than others, thereby reducing their acceptance of automated vehicles for personal use. The study underscores the role of self-serving psychological illusions about the self in the context of automation. Under the assumption that adoption of self-driving vehicles will eventually translate into greatly increased road safety, this article therefore suggests a possible psychological hurdle toward progress and gains in consumer welfare.

Novak and Hoffman (2024) take a different tack, exploring a methodological approach that can help managers develop consumer-facing applications as part of the Internet of Things (IoT). This work offers significant implications for consumer welfare by shedding light on how IoT interaction data can be leveraged to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of automation features (exploitation) and uncover new opportunities for automation capabilities and innovations (exploration). Specifically, they argue that by utilizing IoT interaction data, companies can strike a balance between refining existing automation features and exploring innovative capabilities, leading to the development of more adaptive and intelligent automation systems. These systems, in turn, are poised to evolve alongside consumer needs and technological advancements, thereby offering more personalized, efficient, and innovative solutions to everyday tasks and challenges. Novak and Hoffman’s work directly contributes to consumer welfare by enabling a nuanced understanding of consumer automation interactions. This understanding can guide companies in developing more consumer-centric products and services, enhancing the consumer experience with technology, and fostering a more innovative and responsive market landscape.

content:
Moderators of Consumer Preferences for Automation: Process, Surface, and User Characteristics
One of the most important use cases for algorithms in the service of consumers is as aids to decision making. That can take different shapes, ranging from the ubiquitous recommendation systems in e-commerce platforms to decision support systems and other algorithmic inputs into decision making, from sports betting to weather to financial decision making. This JACR issue features several articles that illuminate the evolving landscape of recommender systems and decision support systems through a multifaceted exploration of how these technologies interface with consumer psychology.

Kim and Lehmann (2024) examine how a consumer’s past consumption variety influences their receptiveness to personalized recommendation services. Consumers enriched by a diverse array of past experiences demonstrate greater openness to technologies that streamline the decision-making process by filtering the plethora of available choices. This correlation underscores the pivotal role of past consumer behavior in shaping future technology adoption. Furthermore, Kim and Lehmann’s additional exploration into the impact of decision difficulty adds another dimension to our understanding. They articulate how the interplay between past variety in consumption and inherent decision-making challenges can modulate the effectiveness of personalized recommendation services. For consumers who naturally find decisions burdensome, the benefits of past variety in enhancing openness to recommendation services are mitigated.

Expanding the discourse, Fei and Dietvorst (2024) study consumer preferences for algorithms that appear to mirror the events they predict. This preference indicates a deeper psychological layer to consumer interactions with technology, where the perceived methodological congruence of an algorithm with the nature of the event it predicts can significantly sway user trust and acceptance, sometimes even taking precedence over accuracy. This article is a powerful example of the importance of going beyond a simplistic dichotomy as typically studied in the “algorithm aversion” literature, where researchers compare consumer responses to the same information provided by human or algorithmic recommenders, a topic we will return to in the future research section below.

Together, these studies paint a fresh picture of the contemporary challenges and opportunities facing the integration of recommender systems and decision support systems into consumer lives. They underscore the importance of considering the interplay between human psychology and technology design in the quest for more seamless, effective, and personalized consumer experiences in the digital age. Usman and colleagues (2024) add to this by exploring human-computer interaction through the lens of a fundamentally interpersonal phenomenon: ingratiation. In a series of studies, they explore the effectiveness of ingratiation in AI-driven products and services. They find that AI ingratiation increases consumer acceptance of product recommendations because of consumers’ self-serving motivations to perceive AI’s flattery as accurate and objective. This effect, however, is moderated by the degree of AI anthropomorphism; human-like AI perceived to ingratiate is more likely to trigger persuasion knowledge and skepticism. Thus, while recent literature has mostly shown how humanizing AI leads to more positive consumer responses (e.g., Yalcin et al. 2022), this article points to the existence of exceptions.

Some of the themes in this research are echoed in other articles in this issue. Regarding the effect of humanizing cues, Bluvstein and colleagues (2024) investigate how typographical errors and their correction during text-based interactions affect perceptions of humanness in communication. The results reveal that customer service agents who make, and then correct, a typo are perceived as more human and helpful compared to agents who make no typos or who make typos but do not correct them. The research emphasizes the importance of error correction in enhancing perceived humanness and helpfulness. Thus, in digital communications, the dynamic process of writing, including making and correcting errors, is used by consumers as a cue for humanness. The findings offer an interesting window into our times. They exemplify the enormous technological progress of recent years; to appear more humanlike, machines nowadays need to simulate lapses and human fallibility.

Zhang, Tuk, and Klesse (2024) take a different approach to explore the role of humanizing AI. Rather than examining effects of anthropomorphizing AI processes or output, they point out that the output of an AI is usually at least partially the result of some form of human input. This could be at the level of conceptualizing, programming, or supervision. For example, AI output is often subject to confirmation or verification by humans, a process often referred to as putting a human in the loop (Cohen et al. 2023). The authors show that making the human input in the generation of AI coaches’ advice salient enhances the perceived helpfulness of that advice as it enhances consumers’ perceived understanding of the AI.

content:
Future Research Directions: Which Algorithms
In recent years, consumer research has been enriched by a sizeable number of studies examining the interplay between psychology and consumer reactions to automation and AI. This scholarly discourse has made significant contributions to our understanding of how psychological predispositions influence the interaction between consumers and technology. However, reflecting the lack of a clear distinction highlighted in the introduction between different types of algorithms in the consumer behavior literature, consumer research has typically not differentiated between the various forms of automation in marketing and consumption—from simple algorithms to AI—and has come to use the terms interchangeably. Research participants are typically confronted with an outcome generated, or said to have been generated, by an automated process, which is referred to as an algorithm or, increasingly, as AI, irrespective of how simple the underlying algorithm may have been. For example, algorithmic approval of financial transactions by financial service providers often still relies on simple decision criteria such as a customer’s account balance (Tomaino et al. 2020). We suggest that the lack of a clear distinction has led consumer researchers to focus on the impact of psychology on how consumers assess and respond to automation, primarily by measuring attitudes toward the use of algorithms versus human intervention in marketing, medical, and legal decision making. Much research in consumer psychology has focused on psychological drivers of algorithm aversion, often expressed as a preference for human decision makers over algorithmic ones. For example, Longoni, Bonezzi, and Morewedge (2019) showed that people’s concern for uniqueness shapes their attitudes toward the use of algorithms in medical contexts.

This issue of JACR points to a change of perspective in contemporary consumer research from comparing consumer preferences for automation versus human intervention to focusing on contextual, functional, or surface characteristics of the deployment of AI that enhance consumer attitudes toward specific types of automation. What may turn into the next phase of research on consumers and automation acknowledges that companies will increasingly force consumers to interact with machines instead of humans, limiting consumers’ choice in the matter. For example, due to cost and scale limitations, for firms wishing to provide advice to consumers the alternative to recommendation algorithms is usually not a personalized recommendation by a human expert but no recommendation at all.

We propose that focusing on the specific functional capabilities of AI—from prediction to problem solving to creation—provides another advantage. It enables researchers to examine the feedback loop between human and artificial intelligence, or the way these diverse types of cognition intersect and mutually influence one another. Shedding light on the interplay between human and artificial intelligence holds profound implications for understanding contemporary consumption patterns, which are increasingly the joint result of two intelligences (Braun et al. 2024). As we live an ever-greater portion of our lives online, we are increasingly making decisions in an environment where crucial choice cues are selected for us by algorithms—little of what you see online you see “just because.” Our choices affect the parameters of the algorithms we interact with and of the algorithms that observe and monitor our behavior. This updating process in turn results in changes in the algorithms’ outputs. And on it goes. This topic is challenging due to its inherently interdisciplinary nature, demanding concerted efforts to bridge the divide between computer science and behavioral science, but consumers researchers will fail to provide an accurate account of human consumption in the digital age unless they engage in such efforts.

Future Research Directions: Which Humans
Focusing on specific types of, or capabilities of, autonomous AI may also allow consumer researchers to ask a rather new type of research question—how machines impact people’s understanding of their own psychology, including, for example, people’s perceptions of their own autonomy (André et al. 2018). We speculate that this research direction will become more pressing if, or when, AI systems emulate more and more aspects of human intelligence and even acquire artificial general intelligence. Moving forward, we call for research to begin exploring the potential insights consumers might gain regarding their own psychology through engagements with AI. As expressed in Yalcin and Puntoni (2023, 132), “Now that people are interacting meaningfully with AI and automated technologies, it’s time to switch our focus from what we think about these technologies to how they make us feel about ourselves.”

Thus, AI could be seen as a reflective surface, akin to the protagonist’s portrait in Oscar Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray. AI may function as a medium through which humans gain deeper insights into their own nature and, potentially, perceived shortcomings. For the first time in our history, humanity faces a form of intelligence that sometimes seems to mirror our own in complexity and capability, evoking an encounter with extraterrestrial intelligence. This unprecedented interaction presents an opportunity for introspection and self-examination. This approach could significantly broaden the scope of discussion in the field, opening new pathways for inquiry into the reciprocal relationship between humanity and the intelligent systems it has created.

content:
Consider, for example, how the historical discourse surrounding human exceptionalism seems to have recently undergone a fascinating shift in both popular and high culture. Previously, when people reflected on what makes humans special, emphasis was often placed on cognitive abilities, because the reference comparison category for humans was other animals and cognitive abilities is what differentiates us from them. However, contemporary discussions of human exceptionalism often pivot toward the realm of emotions and social intelligence because the reference comparison category for humans has now become AI and emotional experience is what differentiates us from it. In other words, as machines start matching our high-order cognitive abilities, we increasingly seek refuge in the experiential and the relational. We expect that in both consumption and work situations, people will increasingly value these aspects of our inner and social lives, with far-reaching implications for choices, well-being, and our self-concept.

Automation for Managers and Consumers
AI increasingly allows marketers to automate elements of the marketing process such as decisions around the 4Ps (product, price, place, and promotion) and consumer-firm interactions. Prediction algorithms trained on large and ever-growing data sets can maximize consumer response rates to product offers, advertising and promotional activities; personalize prices; and optimize shipping and distribution in sync with consumption patterns. Many of these automated marketing activities are referred to as personalization. The recent advent of LLMs and generative AI more generally holds the promise of much more meaningful personalization, with obvious benefits for the efficiency and effectiveness of marketing efforts. In addition to automating marketers’ tasks, companies are also investing heavily in the automation of consumption tasks. Across many product categories, innovations provide consumers with ever greater arrays of automated product features. This creates efficiency gains for consumers; in many ways, the automation of everyday tasks is one of the hallmarks of societal progress, as illustrated by washing machines after WWII or by self-driving cars in the near future.

Despite all these positives emerging from the automation of marketing and consumption activities, automation can also create barriers to adoption for consumers. Beyond individual adoption behavior, automation raises a variety of societal challenges and concerns, several of which are highlighted in the research reported in this issue. We hope that this collection of articles will prove insightful to both scholars and practitioners, and that it will encourage others to explore the boundary between technology and marketing, and what it means to be human in the age of amazing machines.

# About the book
In "A Human's Guide to Machine Intelligence," Wharton professor and tech entrepreneur Kartik Hosanagar explores the pervasive role of algorithms and artificial intelligence in our daily lives. From influencing our shopping choices to determining whom we date, these systems now govern critical decisions that once rested in human hands, such as those made by doctors and judges. Hosanagar delves into the complexities and potential biases of algorithmic decision-making, emphasizing the need for a nuanced understanding of these technologies. Drawing from his professional experience in algorithm design, along with insights from history, computer science, and psychology, he examines real-world examples like Microsoft's controversial chatbot Tay and the challenges of self-driving cars. This engaging and thought-provoking book serves as both a critical analysis of algorithmic impact and a practical guide for navigating the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.

# Chapter 4 Summary : 4. Algorithms Become Intelligent

## 4. Algorithms Become Intelligent

### A Brief History of AI

In a letter to Benjamin Franklin in 1783, Hungarian inventor Wolfgang von Kempelen introduced the Mechanical Turk, a chess-playing automaton that captivated audiences across Europe, despite being a hoax with a hidden human player. This fascination with the dream of artificial intelligence persisted until the mid-20th century when Alan Turing proposed the question "Can machines think?" and introduced the Turing Test to measure machine intelligence. Shortly after, John McCarthy organized the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on AI, which became a landmark event and helped coin the term "artificial intelligence," inspiring significant academic interest.

### Pioneering Developments in AI

[Page 22]
Among the attendees were Herb Simon and Al Newell, who developed the Logic Theorist, the first symbolic AI program, which could prove mathematical theorems. By the late 1960s, Simon advocated that machines would perform any human task within twenty years. In 1967, Mac Hack VI became the first computer to win a game in a human chess tournament. The AI field evolved, with researchers adopting various approaches including rule-based logic and statistical methods. However, neural networks lost favor after critiques outlined their limitations.

## The AI Winter

The 1970s saw disillusionment in AI, termed the "AI winter," as projects failed to meet inflated expectations, leading to reduced funding and public interest. Researchers then shifted focus from artificial general intelligence (AGI) to more practical systems, notably expert systems that operated within narrow domains. Notably, IBM's Deep Blue defeated chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, demonstrating the potential of AI, but expert systems faced limitations due to their rigidity and lack of adaptability.

[Page 23]
## The Resurgence of Machine Learning

As the 2000s began, researchers realized that true
intelligence required algorithms capable of learning from
data. The internet revolution facilitated access to large
datasets, and advancements in processing capabilities and
machine learning techniques fostered a comeback for AI.
Deep learning emerged, leveraging multiple layers of neural
networks to identify complex patterns without explicit
programming.

### Key Examples and Advancements

Examples of successful applications include spam detection
and medical diagnostics. The historical development of a
diagnostic tool like Internist-1 illustrated early Al's
limitations. By contrast, modern systems leverage deep
learning to automatically identify medical conditions from
vast datasets without predefined rules.

### Future Directions and Trade-offs

Both expert systems and machine learning represent
legitimate AI paradigms, each with societal implications and

[Page 24]
trade-offs. The journey from the Mechanical Turk to
advanced machine learning illustrates profound changes in
the quest for artificial intelligence, raising questions about
the future trajectory of this dynamic field.

The origins of human temperament and behavior have been debated for centuries, with various philosophers and scientists attributing influences to either genetic inheritance (nature) or environmental factors (nurture). The idea that both elements play a vital role has gained traction, highlighted by twin studies, which isolate genetic influences from environmental ones.

Twins are instrumental in understanding the nature-nurture debate, as identical twins share the same genes, while fraternal twins share about half. Studies have shown that traits like intelligence and personality are impacted by both genes and environment, with significant findings that affirm neither side dominates entirely.

Modern algorithms learn from data similar to how humans learn from their environment, leading to behavior influenced by both their programming (nature) and the data they are trained on (nurture). ## Chapter 7: In Algorithms We Trust

### Introduction

This chapter discusses the dichotomy in public trust toward algorithms, particularly in high-stakes scenarios like self-driving cars and investment management. It opens with the tragic incident involving Joshua Brown, who was killed while using the Autopilot feature in his Tesla, raising questions about trust in technology.

### The Tesla Incident

In May 2016, Joshua Brown's Tesla, in Autopilot mode, tragically crashed into a semi-truck, resulting in his death. This incident sparked widespread debate about the safety of self-driving technology. Critics highlighted that Tesla's Autopilot was still in beta testing and the need for drivers to

[Page 34]
remain engaged.

## Public Perception of Algorithms

Despite the potential safety benefits of self-driving cars,
public opinion remains skeptical. Surveys indicate that many
people still trust human drivers over automated systems,
reflecting a preference for human intuition and experience.
Conversely, automated investment platforms like Betterment
gained popularity as people increasingly trusted algorithms
with their financial management.

## Trust in Algorithms: Factors Influencing Perception

1.
**Performance Evidence**
: Public trust is influenced by the perceived performance of
algorithms compared to humans. Many people do not trust
self-driving cars as they believe humans are more reliable,
despite evidence suggesting that autonomous vehicles could
be safer.

2.
**Better-Than-Average Effect**

[Page 35]
: People tend to believe they are better than average drivers, contributing to their reluctance to trust automated systems.
3.
**Complexity of Tasks**
: There is skepticism surrounding the ability of algorithms to handle novel situations, although advances in machine learning challenge this notion.
4.
**Dehumanization Concerns**
: The rise of algorithmic decision-making in contexts like hiring raises ethical concerns about reducing individuals to numbers, which can affect trust levels.

## Observing Algorithm Performance

Research indicates that when individuals observe algorithms making mistakes, their trust in those algorithms diminishes significantly. Instances where human forecasters make errors do not evoke the same level of distrust, demonstrating a bias against machines.

## Implications for Self-Driving and Medical Algorithms

[Page 36]
Following the Tesla crash and a subsequent fatal incident involving a self-driving Uber, public sentiment shifted further away from trusting autonomous vehicles. In the medical field, the introduction of algorithms in radiology has been met with mixed results, as initial systems did not outperform human experts and led to increased rates of unnecessary biopsies.

## Evolving Trust in Medical Algorithms

Recent advancements in deep learning algorithms show promise in medical diagnostics. However, the failures of earlier systems have created skepticism among professionals about adopting new technologies. Some experts believe that, rather than replacing healthcare professionals, algorithms will augment their capabilities.

## Conclusion

The future of algorithms in driving and medical fields hinges on public trust. For algorithms and AI systems to be effectively integrated, overcoming the initial mistrust arising from negative experiences is crucial. As technology evolves, so must our understanding and acceptance of its capabilities

open arms rather than skepticism.

## Inside the Black Box

## Introduction

The chapter explores the complexity of trusting algorithms, especially in contexts like healthcare, where AI systems influence critical decisions. The author emphasizes that effective communication about algorithms' workings fosters trust, yet achieving transparency is far from straightforward.

## The Dilemma of Trust in Algorithms

A fictional narrative illustrates a patient struggling to trust an AI-driven health diagnosis. The character's hesitance to follow medical advice underscores the importance of understanding how algorithms derive their conclusions. Transparency, as research indicates, is vital for trust.

[Page 42]
## The Case of Clifford Nass

Nass faced student complaints in his class due to grading inconsistencies among teaching assistants (TAs). Rather than address the issues simply, he developed an algorithm to adjust grades based on scoring tendencies. However, his detailed explanation of the adjustments led to student dissatisfaction rather than trust, highlighting the intricate relationship between transparency and user trust.

## Insight from Kizilcec's Experiment

René Kizilcec conducted experiments to understand how different levels of transparency affect trust in a grading algorithm. His findings revealed that mere transparency is insufficient; the nature of information—referred to as how, why, and trade-off explanations—greatly influences trust levels.

## The Need for an Algorithmic Bill of Rights

- Just as dissenters like George Mason pushed for protections of individual rights during the formation of the U.S. Constitution, today's digital landscape demands safeguards against the unchecked power of algorithmic systems.
- Incorporation of lessons from the past can inform the development of guidelines for artificial intelligence (AI).

## Existing Recommendations and Guidelines

- Reports like the White House's "Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence" outline challenges posed by AI and provide recommendations, though many are vague.
- Organizations such as ACM and the AI Now Institute propose guiding principles for ethical AI deployment, advocating for accountability, transparency, and user rights.

speaks to the urgent necessity for ethical oversight in
technology.

**Critical Interpretation:** This proposition underscores the
parallel between historical safeguards for individual
rights, as seen during the formation of the U.S.

algorithms. While Hosanagar argues for such a

insufficient without robust, multifaceted frameworks

dynamics inherent in algorithmic systems.

## Conclusion: The Games Algorithms Play

> In life, unlike chess, the game continues after checkmate. — Isaac Asimov

## The Significance of Story in AI

Historian David Nye emphasizes that "the meaning of a tool is inseparable from the stories that surround it," particularly in AI, where narratives often center around games. The fascination with chess and similar games has long influenced Al development, beginning with Kempelen's Mechanical Turk, a chess-playing automaton that, though a hoax, sparked significant interest in AI capabilities. Many believed that once machines could master chess—considered the pinnacle of intellectual challenge—AI would have achieved a major milestone.

## Chess as a Catalyst for AI Research

[Page 50]
Chess has been described as the "drosophila of artificial
intelligence," serving as a simplified environment for testing
ideas. Just as fruit flies have advanced genetics research,
chess has been a critical testing ground for AI concepts. The
excitement peaked when IBM's Deep Blue defeated Garry
Kasparov in 1997, marking a significant moment in AI
recognition. However, as time progressed, critics questioned
the implications of this achievement and the narrow focus on
games as the measure of intelligence.

## Broader Perspectives on AI Development

Critics like John McCarthy and Rodney Brooks urged a shift
away from gaming as the sole focus of AI research,
advocating for technology that tackles real-world tasks. The
obsession with quantifiable game success has kept
researchers from exploring more complex and practical
applications of AI.

## The Next AI Milestones: Beyond Games

Following chess, Jeopardy! became the next benchmark with
IBM's Watson, which showcased capabilities beyond mere

[Page 51]
symbol manipulation. The success of AI continued with
Google's DeepMind creating AlphaGo, which defeated Go
champion Lee Sedol. These developments prompted
speculation about future challenges that could push AI
further.

## Envisioning General-Purpose AI

Nils Nilsson proposed a measure of AI success beyond
games, suggesting that mastering a variety of jobs could
indicate real human-level intelligence. Studies suggest that
almost half of occupations could be automated with existing
technology, hinting at an imminent change in workforce
dynamics.

## Human Decision-Making: The Key Frontier

While software outperforms humans on many tasks, the
essence of human intelligence in decision-making is
increasingly being explored by AI. As AI expands into these
areas, there is a pressing need for establishing rights and
regulations to navigate this evolving landscape.

groundwork for future developments in AI.

think inspired the field of artificial intelligence. His proposed
'Turing test' established a benchmark for assessing machine

conversation indistinguishable from a human, thus framing
foundational inquiries into the nature of thinking and
intelligence.

officially recognized artificial intelligence as a distinct
scientific field and coined the term 'AI.' It brought together
leading minds who established necessary frameworks and
goals for AI research, inspiring subsequent advancements
and implicating the pursuit of human-level intelligence in
machines.

# Chapter 5 | 5. Machine Learning and the Predictability-Resilience Paradox| Q&A

**1.Question**
What is the predictability-resilience paradox in machine
learning?
**Answer:** The predictability-resilience paradox refers
to the trade-off between creating highly predictable
algorithms that follow clear rules and thus can
perform reliably in known environments, versus
creating resilient algorithms that can adapt to new,
complex, and unpredictable real-world scenarios but
become more difficult to understand and anticipate
in their behavior.

**2.Question**

[Page 92]

Answer:AlphaGo didn't rely on pre-defined human
strategies; instead, it utilized machine learning techniques to
develop its own strategies by analyzing millions of past Go
games and playing against itself millions of times, leading to
an emergent form of creativity that could mimic human-like
decision-making.

**3.Question**
How does the story of Don Swanson illustrate the power
of cross-disciplinary knowledge in scientific discovery?
Answer:Don Swanson, an information scientist, discovered a
potential treatment for Raynaud's syndrome by linking
seemingly unrelated studies about fish oil's effects on blood
flow. His example shows that uncovering significant insights
often requires connecting disparate fields of knowledge,
something that traditional expert systems may overlook.

**4.Question**
What lesson does the juxtaposition of the Code of
Hammurabi and the U.S. Constitution teach us about
decision-making systems?

[Page 93]
Answer:The Code of Hammurabi represents a predictable,
rigid decision-making framework that becomes obsolete over
time, whereas the U.S. Constitution embodies adaptability
and the ability to evolve, highlighting that resilient systems
are better equipped to survive changing circumstances.

# Chapter 6 | 6. The Psychology of Algorithms| Q&A
**1.Question**
What causes algorithms to behave unexpectedly, as seen
with Microsoft's Tay and XiaoIce?
**Answer:**The behavior of algorithms can be
attributed to two main factors: their programming
(nature) and the data they are exposed to (nurture).
Tay behaved offensively due to the inappropriate
language and sentiments she learned from her
interactions on Twitter, while XiaoIce thrived in a
structured environment that reinforced affection
and warmth in conversation.

**2.Question**
How does the nature versus nurture debate apply to
human behavior and algorithms?

[Page 97]
Answer:Both genetics (nature) and environmental influences (nurture) are significant in shaping behavior. In humans, studies show that traits like intelligence can stem from genetics, but factors such as upbringing and social environment also play crucial roles. Similarly, algorithms learn and display behaviors based on their coding and the contexts in which they learn, leading to variable outcomes.

**3.Question**
Can you provide an example illustrating the impact of nurture on algorithmic behavior?
Answer:The stark contrast between Tay and XiaoIce serves as a prime example. While Tay was exposed to the chaotic and often abusive language prevalent on Twitter, XiaoIce learned from the more controlled and supportive conversations in Chinese social networks, which made her responses warm and socially acceptable.

**4.Question**
What role do twins studies play in understanding behavior, both human and algorithmic?

[Page 98]
Answer:Twin studies help isolate the effects of genetics and environment on behavior. They show that identical twins raised apart can still exhibit similar traits, indicating the influence of genetics, while also highlighting how differing environments shape their experiences. In the context of algorithms, the differences between similarly designed algorithms operating in different environments (like Tay and XiaoIce) can show how nurture affects their outcomes.

**5.Question**
How might the findings on twin studies inform the development of algorithms?
Answer:Twin studies highlight the importance of both nature and nurture in shaping behavior, suggesting that when designing algorithms, creators should consider both the inherent logic of the algorithm and the data it processes. Understanding that the environment significantly influences behavior can lead to more robust and ethical algorithm design.

# The Age of AI

"It's a Rembrandt!"

So shouted the neatly dressed, white-haired gentleman after quickly raising his hand. Several other members of the audience called out in agreement. One man, who ran a leading art museum in Australia, said he recognized the unique style of the seventeenth-century Dutch master, but he seemed puzzled that he couldn't recall this specific painting, shown in figure 1-1.

**FIGURE 1-1**

**The next Rembrandt**

[IMAGE: A black and white portrait of a man in 17th-century Dutch style, wearing a large black hat and a white ruffled collar.]

*Source:* reproduced by permission of ING and J. Walter Thompson.

Then a video began to play, and the room fell silent as the narrator described the work's provenance.↓ The portrait, it turns out, was not a Rembrandt. Rather, it was created in 2016 by a team from advertising agency J. Walter Thompson and Microsoft as a promotion for ING Group, the Dutch bank. The painting consists of more than 148 million pixels, based on 168,263 scans of Rembrandt's three hundred known paintings. A team of data

[Page 7]
scientists, engineers, and Rembrandt experts applied learning algorithms to
analyze the portraits and select specific characteristics that were typical in
some way of the artist's work: they determined that the new painting would
feature a Caucasian male between the ages of thirty and forty, with facial
hair; he would wear a hat and a white collar; and he would face to the right.
More algorithms were used to assemble the components into a fully formed
composition. A 3-D printer then deposited thirteen layers of paint-based UV
ink on a canvas in a way that closely imitated the master's brushstrokes.
Thus *The Next Rembrandt*, as the work is called, came into being via
artificial intelligence—some 350 years after the artist's death.
Al is becoming a force in the arts, connecting various disciplines and media
and expanding the range of artistic possibilities. With its Arts and Machine
Intelligence (AMI) program, for example, Google is organizing a community
of artists and engineers to explore how creative practices are being
transformed. The community applies the kinds of style-transfer techniques
used in *The Next Rembrandt* across a broad variety of subjects and media,
from film to music.
But AMI and other similar programs are taking AI even further into the realm
of creation: in addition to replicating existing styles, Al is being used to
create completely new works of art. This endeavor transforms not only the
method for crafting the work of art but also the organization and process that
conceives and creates it. Ahmed Elgammal, director of the Art & Artificial
Intelligence Lab at Rutgers University, is working with an art-generating
algorithm called AICAN that is programmed to produce novelty without
substantial help from human artists. The program starts with training data
drawn from a vast assemblage of paintings dating from the fourteenth century
and produces something fundamentally different: paintings “inspired" by
established artistic styles but entirely new. Thus, the AI algorithms do not
merely expand the range of creation and distribution methods for artists; they
also model the course of art history, offering insight into art's long
progression from figuration to abstraction and helping us understand
processes that have been running in the collective unconscious for more than
half a millennium.
This is only the beginning. If a computer, aided by a few computer scientists
and some fairly basic AI, can simulate, collaborate with, or possibly even
extend the work of creative genius, we can almost guarantee that no field of
human endeavor will remain independent of artificial intelligence. In
discipline after discipline and industry after industry, digital networks and AI
are becoming pervasive, defining a new age for business and for all of us.

# Competing in the Age of Al

[Page 8]
> AI is the “runtime" that is going to shape all of what we do.  
> —Satya Nadella, Microsoft CEO

Al is becoming the universal engine of execution. As digital technology increasingly shapes “all of what we do" and enables a rapidly growing number of tasks and processes, Al is becoming the new operational foundation of business—the core of a company's operating model, defining how the company drives the execution of tasks. Al is not only displacing human activity, it is changing the very concept of the firm.

As such, the first truly dramatic implications of artificial intelligence may be less a function of simulating human nature and more a function of transforming the nature of organizations and the ways they shape the world around us.

This book describes the profound implications of artificial intelligence for business. It is transforming the very nature of companies—how they operate and how they compete. When a business is driven by AI, software instructions and algorithms make up the critical path in the way the firm delivers value. This is the “runtime"—the environment that shapes the execution of all processes—that Nadella refers to. In a digital operating model, humans may have designed the operational systems, but computers are actually doing the work in real time: painting the digital Rembrandt, setting a price on Amazon, recommending a product on Walmart's mobile app, qualifying a customer for an Ant Financial loan—all processes that would traditionally have required human intelligence, not only to design but also to execute.

Having software shape the critical path of operational execution has substantial ramifications. Digital, Al-driven processes are more scalable than traditional processes. They enable greater scope (or variety), as they easily connect with a myriad of other digitized businesses, and they create powerful opportunities for learning and improvement, such as the ability to produce ever more accurate, complex, and sophisticated predictions and even gain fundamental understanding. In doing so, networks and Al are reshaping the operational foundations of firms, enabling digital scale, scope, and learning, and erasing deep-seated limits that have constrained firm growth and impact for hundreds of years.

We are already there, and the AI that is driving the explosive growth of firms like Facebook and Tencent isn't even all that sophisticated. To bring about the kinds of dramatic changes we're describing, AI need not be indistinguishable from human behavior, or capable of simulating human reasoning—what is sometimes referred to as strong AI. We need only a computer system to perform tasks that were traditionally performed by

[Page 9]
human beings, in what is traditionally referred to as weak Al. We don't need
a perfect human replica to prioritize content on a social network, make a
perfect cappuccino, analyze customer behavior, set the optimal price, or even,
apparently, paint in the style of Rembrandt. Imperfect, weak Al is already
enough to transform the nature of firms and how they operate.
Even with relatively basic artificial intelligence, whose applications we have
seen explode over the past ten years, we are witnessing unprecedented
changes. We have entered a new age in which networks and algorithms are
woven into the fabric of the firm, changing how industries function and the
way the economy operates. Across both new and old enterprises, digital
savvy can no longer be treated as a discrete set of skills and AI can no longer
be viewed as the purview of a specific job description or business function.
Understanding the new opportunities and challenges has become essential to
all of us. And in this new age of AI, many time-honored assumptions about
strategy and leadership no longer apply.

## Transforming Competition

As we enter the age of artificial intelligence, the emergence of digital
operating models is transforming competition. Consider the case of
photography. More than a hundred years ago, the invention of photography
had a disruptive impact on the "technology" of painting by greatly reducing
the demand for such work. Painters had trouble responding to this threat, but
eventually they changed their approaches, inventing new techniques and
styles. The important point here is that film-based photography threatened
old norms and created new opportunities, but it did not dramatically
transform the economy. The battle between film photography and painting
resembled the pattern observed across a variety of industries, from disk
drives to excavating machines, when one technological trajectory becomes
disrupted by another.¹ The new overtakes the old, creating challenges for
existing competitors, while the rest of the economy continues more or less as
it was.
In contrast, let's look at what happened when digital photography came on
the scene. With the invention of the first digital camera in 1975 (by Steven
Sasson at Kodak), photographs could be captured as files of stored data that
could be displayed and enhanced on a computer. Early digital photographs
were blurry and expensive. Over time they became sharper and cheaper. Then
they began to threaten traditional photography in a way at first similar to
what a disruptive technology would do: undermining traditional players and
creating opportunities for new businesses.
But digitizing photography did not simply provide an alternative to an older
technology the way smaller disk drives disrupted the demand for larger disk

[Page 10]
drives. Digital representation completely transformed the nature and variety
of activities connected to photography. It was suddenly easy and free to share
pictures (benefiting from digital automation at essentially zero marginal
cost), so people started snapping and sharing many more photos. No event,
no activity, no meal is now too trivial to document and post on social media.
This practice gave rise to a new breed of companies—Facebook, Tencent,
Snapchat, Line, and TikTok are just a few of them—each of them featuring
massively scalable digital operating models to help users select, shape, and
share digital representations of their lives and of the world around them.
Increasingly sophisticated Al is dramatically expanding the impact of
photography's transformation. Think of the vast number of photos being
taken every day (now more than 10 trillion digital photographs each year,
five orders of magnitude greater than the total number of traditional
photographs ever taken) as a growing dataset—most of it now stored in the
cloud on Google, Facebook, and WeChat, where it can be analyzed by
algorithms. These troves are powering the improvement of algorithms used
for facial recognition, photo sorting, and image enhancement. With the help
of the additional data already available to them, and a little bit of “training,”
social platforms like Google, Facebook, and WeChat can automatically
identify (even predict) not only family and friends but also affinities (are the
people in this shot members of the same family?) and backgrounds (is this
person a schoolmate?). Photo apps are already recommending products,
services, and even news feeds that users might like and some are making
friend recommendations—offering to “introduce” you to someone based on
shared affinities or backgrounds.
When digital technology collided with traditional photography, it did not
simply replace it with something cheaper, more differentiated, or higher
quality. It did not merely create a new value proposition to serve customers.
It enabled the emergence of a new and increasingly powerful breed of
company, one that leverages a different kind of operating model and
competes in different ways. In doing so, it not only changed the photography
industry but reshaped the world around it. This is because when an activity is
digitized (like converting a paint stroke into pixels), profound changes take
place. A digital representation is infinitely scalable—it is now possible to
easily and perfectly communicate the pattern it represents, replicate it, and
transmit it at virtually zero marginal cost to a near infinite numbers of
recipients, anywhere in the world. Moreover, digitizing the activity makes it
easily connectable, also at zero marginal cost, to limitless other,
complementary activities, dramatically increasing its scope. Finally, the
digital activity can embed processing instructions—AI algorithms that shape
behavior and enable a variety of possible paths and responses. This logic can
learn as it processes data, continuously training and improving the algorithms

[Page 11]
that are embedded in it. The digital representation of a human activity can
thus learn and improve itself in ways that analog processes cannot. These
factors completely transform the ways a firm can (and should) operate.
Traditionally, the intrinsic scalability, scope amplification, and learning
potential of technology was limited by the operating architecture of the
organizations that it was deployed in. But over the past decade, we have seen
the emergence of firms that are designed and architected to release the full
potential of digital networks, data, algorithms, and AI. Indeed, the more a
firm is designed to optimize the impact of digitization, the greater its
potential for scale, scope, and learning embedded in its operating model—
and the more value it can create and capture (see figure 1-2). Increasing
levels of digitization, analytics, and AI/ML can dramatically improve the
scalability of a business, making the value curve increase more rapidly as a
function of the number of users or their engagement. As it collides with a
traditional company, a digital operating model can overwhelm the status quo.
The first losers were the traditional players that could not adapt. Ultimately,
Kodak was not killed by Fuji or by a digital photography startup, but by the
emergence of smartphone and social network firms. Instead of focusing on
industry-level tasks like film processing and marketing, Facebook, Tencent,
and Google focused on connecting users and on capturing and analyzing the
information that flows through their networks. These firms create value
differently, capture value differently, and rely on a completely different kind
of operating model from Kodak's to deliver that value to their customers. The
result is a fundamentally different way to compete. These companies never
even considered Kodak a competitor; rather the film company was simply
collateral damage in the newer companies' race to acquire users on networks
that enabled photo sharing as a core service.

**FIGURE 1-2**

**The collision between traditional and digital operating models**

But the story does not end there. Just as the social and mobile platforms
reached unprecedented levels of scale, scope, and learning, we began to
discover that digital operating models introduced a new set of challenges
while they crushed traditional competitors. Their unconstrained growth and
unrestrained impact raised new risks. From privacy to cybersecurity, and
from bias to fake news, the rise of the AI-driven firm is posing new kinds of
threats. Traditionally, corporate leaders faced a bounded set of challenges,
constrained by the relatively limited impact of their organizations on the
surrounding economy, environment, and social system. Without the same

[Page 12]
intrinsic limits on scalability, scope, and impact, the new breed of digital firm
requires new approaches to leadership, regulation, and even ethics.

## *Alexa, How Do You Transform the Economy?*

Perhaps more than any other organization, Amazon embodies the way an
organization can leverage a digital operating model to transform traditional
industries. Amazon sells real things—goods and services we need every
day—and in doing so it collides with all the businesses that have been selling
those goods and services in the same way for generations. Amazon reinvents
traditional business operations and puts them on digital foundations. In doing
so it harvests the advantages of digital technology, analytics, and AI/ML in
order to scale, extend its scope, and learn. And by colliding with traditional
businesses, from books to consumer electronics to groceries, Amazon
changes the rules of competition.

In a traditional business, size is a double-edged sword. As it grows, a
business can usually deliver more value at a cheaper price. However, the
advantages of scale tend to be limited by the firm's operating model, which
encompasses all the assets and processes it uses to deliver the value it
promises to its customers. As the firm gets bigger, its operating model
becomes increasingly complex, and with complexity come all kinds of
problems. Think of the long lines in your favorite retail store when there are
too many customers, or the confusion that emerges when a rapidly growing
firm hires too many new employees, or the quality problems that plague a
manufacturing plant when demands for capacity or product variety are
increased. Ultimately, complexity becomes the downfall of traditional
organizations, increasing operational costs and decreasing service levels. All
this despite the fact that dealing with operational complexity is the goal of
many of the managerial and administrative systems developed over the past
one hundred years, from the assembly line to the multidivisional company
structure.

But when Amazon digitizes an operating task it embraces the advantages
of digital scale, scope, and learning. Its digital systems scale more easily and
continue to improve despite the size and complexity of its operation. When
the order-taking system is fully digitized, it does not become harder to
manage as more consumers use it, or as they demand more variety; it just
gets better and better. As an increasing portion of the processes and tasks that
deliver customer value are digitized, the advantages increase to create a much
more scalable enterprise, capable of delivering an unprecedented scope of
products and services, all characterized by an impressive rate of improvement
and pinpointed targeting.

[Page 13]
Take product suggestions. In traditional retail, product suggestions are made by employees in stores, but their numbers are limited by traditional recruitment and training processes along with personnel budgets. Getting the right sales expertise, furthermore, is difficult: people who are good at selling fishing rods aren't typically good at selling baby clothes. But the algorithm that creates suggestions on the Amazon website does not suffer from the same limitations. The system ingests huge amounts of data on what previous customers bought, and which product purchases were related to each other (for example, purchases that were together in the same shopping cart). The system processes all that data, factoring in product specifications and customer characteristics to suggest new, potentially appealing products. The engine learns and improves with the behavior of every relevant consumer and every relevant product—the more data, and the more scale and product diversity, the better, and Amazon's performance continues to improve. Al engines like Amazon's collaborative filtering algorithms do not incur human complexity costs like communication or coordination. The system does not decrease in efficiency as it grows and is thus much more scalable than a human (or organizational) learning engine. In addition, it connects easily across applications; much of what Amazon learns from a consumer's book preferences can be applied to suggestions of videos, clothing, or almost anything else.

The key to Amazon is its increasingly digital operating model. Amazon's operating philosophy centers on digitizing the best understanding of operational excellence through the broad-based application of artificial intelligence and machine learning, advanced robotics, and the instantiation of as much know-how as possible into software. In a traditional warehouse, people manage and carry out the process, with the organization suffering the same limitations we see in product suggestions. Not at Amazon. People are secondary in many of the most critical workflows. From demand forecasting to warehouse management, and from supply chain management to capacity planning, software and Al are increasingly running the show. Amazon does employ many people but deploys most of them on the edge of the digital network, doing things that computers are not yet capable of handling (such as picking an oddly shaped product from the warehouse shelf), while at the same time minimizing managerial complexity and maximizing the impact of digital scalability. And many times, computers are defining what humans should do, not the other way around, as in figuring out the optimal path to find and pick a specific product in the warehouse.

Over and over, Amazon has collided with traditional industrial settings and transformed them with a digitized, automated, and increasingly AI-capable alternative. Amazon's service improves with volume, whereas the traditional

[Page 14]
business runs into complexity costs. As Amazon grows, the traditional
business loses out and the industry is transformed.
Echo, Amazon's smart speaker and microphone, extends the company's
strategy to a new range of applications by utilizing Alexa, a voice interface to
the company's AI platform. Echo started by understanding simple, almost
trivial commands, such as “Alexa, play Rage Against The Machine” on
Amazon's music service. The technology improved quickly as it gathered
increasing quantities and types of data and used that data to train itself. As its
functionality increases and improves over time, the Echo-Alexa duo
continues to collide with and transform many traditional tasks, from ordering
vitamins to reading books, and from ordering a car service to controlling
home systems.
The Alexa service, furthermore, is designed as a true hub, with the potential
to connect the user to a virtually limitless array of services and products. As
of September 2018, Alexa had more than fifty thousand skills (actions that it
could perform via voice command) developed by a large ecosystem of third-
party developers.² And as Echo continues on its course, the number of human
needs that can be addressed by an Amazon-provided or -brokered solution
will only continue to increase. Every time you tell Alexa about things you
need to buy, Amazon Echo will build a shopping list and send you the items.
And every time you return and exchange items, Amazon's algorithms will
keep on learning and honing its ability to predict what you need.
Amazon's model is scaling spectacularly well. The company spurred
collisions between analog and digital models in industries from apparel to
computing, and from consumer products to entertainment, threatening
traditional stalwarts from Walmart to Comcast. In the process, Amazon has
become one of the quintessential drivers of industry transformation. It has
changed the way people shop across the globe and raised the expectation of
personalization across the entire array of consumer products and services. As
it reaches scale in more of its markets, from books to groceries, its impact
and market capitalization continue to soar.
As it continues to grow and transform, Amazon is facing increasing scrutiny
from communities and regulators. Given its broad reach among many
traditionally defined markets, its model is not easily challenged by existing
antitrust practices. Sustainable growth will hinge on Amazon leadership's
ability to balance its many consumer benefits against the dislocations it might
force on the rest of the economy. At the same time, Amazon's competitors
are not standing still.
